strengths: Technically solid integration of known components (shortcut flow matching, masked conditioning for in/outpainting, contrastive sync features) into a coherent V2A system, with the first application of the shortcut objective to video-to-audio, enabling few-step sampling without distillation or retraining

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art DeSync (0.497) and best human-eval synchronization (3.52) vs. MMAudio and FoleyCrafter, with competitive FAD/KL and human overall quality despite a smaller model (643M vs. 1.03B)

Well-designed ablation (Table 2) showing shortcut training incurs no quality loss at full step counts, and Figure 5 demonstrating graceful degradation at 8 steps and robustness beyond 20-second generations where MMAudio degrades sharply
Includes a blind, randomized human listening study (18 participants, 180 ratings) covering overall fit, synchronization, and audio quality, with a careful interface described in Appendix A.3

Honest limitations section (quality gap to MMAudio, long-form issues across scene cuts), detailed implementation and training hyperparameters in the appendix, and a new interpretable spectral metric (SWSD) with full algorithmic specification
weaknesses: Limited baseline coverage: Table 1 compares only against FoleyCrafter and MMAudio; Diff-Foley, Frieren, V-AURA, and LoVA are discussed in related work but not empirically compared, and the long-form comparison is only against MMAudio with a modified (arguably favorable) conditioning procedure that the authors themselves only hypothesize helps

Evaluation uses a self-composed test set (in-the-wild videos + VGGSound + UnAV-100) without a clearly specified protocol, making it difficult to verify comparability with previously reported numbers; no statistical significance testing is reported for the small human study

Reproducibility concerns: the paper relies on a proprietary ~5k-hour high-fidelity studio Foley dataset and a fine-tuned 43 Hz Stable-Audio VAE, and the 'Samples are available at' link is blank with no code release stated, which limits others from reliably building on or verifying the contribution

Originality is incremental: the generative objective (Frans et al. 2025), masked conditioning (Chen et al. 2025), architecture (MMDiT-X), and sync-model recipe (SigLIP-style contrastive alignment) are all adapted from prior work; the batch-size analysis for contrastive training (Section 3.1) is anecdotal and not supported by an ablation
The claimed advantage in audio quality is not established: MMAudio wins KL_PANNs, IS, and human audio quality; the suggestion that scaling up would close the gap is speculative and unverified

strengths: The paper addresses practically relevant limitations of current video-to-audio models: long-form generation, audio conditioning/outpainting, and few-step sampling, and combines these in a single coherent system.

The empirical evaluation is multi-faceted, combining objective metrics (FAD, KL, IB, DeSync) with a blind, randomized human listening study including three rating dimensions, and an ablation (Table 2) isolating the effect of the shortcut objective.

The synchronization feature training with a large pretrained video backbone (VideoPrism) and the analysis of batch-size effects on hard negatives for fine-grained sync learning (Section 3.1) is an interesting empirical observation.

The appendix provides a good level of implementation detail (hyperparameters, architecture composition, VAE fine-tuning, evaluation interface), and the proposed SWSD spectral metric is clearly specified with pseudocode.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging the subjective quality gap relative to MMAudio and the fragility of progressive outpainting across scene cuts.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients are all adopted from prior work — shortcut training (Frans et al., 2025), masked in/outpainting flow matching (Chen et al., 2025; VampNet-style mask tokens), MMDiT-X architecture (Esser et al., 2024), and SigLIP-style contrastive sync features (following Synchformer/MMAudio). The contribution is largely an engineering combination of known techniques applied to a new domain, without new analysis of why the combination works.

The central comparative evidence is weakened by a non-standard, self-constructed test set (mix of in-the-wild videos, VGGSound test, and UnAV-100) rather than established V2A benchmarks, making the claimed SOTA results hard to verify or compare against the broader literature, and hurting reproducibility.

The long-form comparison (Figure 5, right) appears favorable by construction: MMAudio is given only a 0.5 s reference while SALSA-V receives 10 s of context, and MMAudio degrades beyond its training length. The authors acknowledge this asymmetry but the headline claim of 'outperforming previous methods in long-form generation' rests largely on this uneven protocol.

The human study is small (18 participants, 180 total scores, 10 videos) with no statistical significance testing reported; the overall-quality gap over MMAudio (3.43 vs 3.29) and the audio-quality deficit (2.96 vs 3.16) may not be meaningful at this sample size, yet the abstract claims the model 'significantly outperforms' prior methods.
Objective results are mixed rather than dominant: MMAudio still wins on KL_PANNs and IS, and matches on IB; the narrative of broad superiority overstates what Table 1 shows.

The claimed 'unconstrained length' generation is qualified in the limitations: iterative outpainting struggles across scene cuts and effectively requires manual intervention (re-seeding, guidance tuning) — the practical long-form capability is narrower than advertised.

No code or model release is evident (the samples link is empty in the manuscript), which, combined with a proprietary in-the-wild training collection and a custom test set, substantially limits reproducibility and the ability of others to build on the work.
Several design choices are justified only post-hoc or anecdotally (e.g., batch size of 28 for contrastive training, 25% consistency ratio, CFG of 4.0) without ablations supporting them.

strengths: The paper tackles practically important limitations of current video-to-audio models: few-step sampling, long-form generation, and audio conditioning. The integration of a shortcut objective directly into flow-matching training (avoiding a separate distillation/reflow stage) is a notable and useful contribution to the V2A domain, and Table 2 provides a reasonable ablation showing the shortcut objective does not degrade quality at full step counts.

The masked flow-matching training objective enabling in-/outpainting and audio-conditioned generation is a sensible mechanism for iterative long-form extension, and the quantitative analysis (Figure 6, SWSD metric in Appendix A.2) supports the claim that conditioning transfers spectral characteristics.

The custom contrastive synchronization model built on a large pretrained VideoPrism backbone is well motivated, and the empirical results are strong: state-of-the-art DeSync (0.497 vs 0.521 for MMAudio) corroborated by the highest human synchronization MOS (3.52), with competitive FAD/KL despite a smaller parameter count (643M vs 1.03B).

Evaluation covers multiple axes (objective metrics, few-step and long-form regimes, audio conditioning, and a blind human study), and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail (training hyperparameters, architecture, VAE fine-tuning, listening-test protocol).
The limitations section is honest and specific, acknowledging the audio-quality gap to MMAudio and the scene-cut weakness of progressive outpainting rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the three core ingredients (shortcut loss from Frans et al. 2025, masked flow matching for in/outpainting closely following Chen et al. 2025, and contrastive sync features following Synchformer) are existing techniques adapted to V2A. The contribution is a well-executed integration rather than a new method, and the claim of being the 'first adoption in the larger field of general generative audio' needs firmer support.

The evaluation relies on a self-constructed test set (in-the-wild videos + VGGSound test + UnAV-100) rather than a standard benchmark. The paper does not specify how baseline models (MMAudio, FoleyCrafter) were configured on this set (caption source, guidance, sampling settings), so the comparison may not be fully apples-to-apples.

The human study is small: 18 participants, 10 videos, 180 total scores, and no statistical significance testing is reported. Given the overall-quality gap is 3.43 vs 3.29 (and audio quality 2.96 vs 3.16 in MMAudio's favor), the claimed human-evaluation advantage rests on weak statistical footing.

The long-form comparison in Figure 5 (right) compares against MMAudio operating outside its training length distribution, with the authors themselves hypothesizing about MMAudio's failure mode. There is no comparison to dedicated long-form baselines such as LoVA or V-AURA, so the long-form claim is demonstrated mainly against a disadvantaged competitor.

Main-table results report no variance across seeds or runs; only the few-step/long-form plots show confidence bands. The batch-size-28 claim for contrastive training is asserted by analogy to Synchformer without an ablation in this paper.

Reproducibility is limited: the sample link is blank in the manuscript, no code release is stated, and key data (in-house Foley set, filtered in-the-wild YouTube collection) are not releasable. This makes independent verification difficult.

The long-form mechanism (iterative outpainting with a ~10s context and 0.5s prepend) is described at a high level; failure behavior at scene cuts, error accumulation over many extension steps, and guidance tuning for conditioning are only briefly discussed in limitations.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of techniques for V2A: the paper is, to the authors' knowledge (and plausibly so), the first to adopt shortcut-model training in the video-to-audio / generative audio domain, enabling native few-step sampling without distillation, which is a genuinely useful contribution distinct from post-hoc distillation (e.g., Frieren's reflow).

The masked flow-matching objective cleanly unifies audio conditioning, in/outpainting, and iterative long-form extension within a single training paradigm, and the design (masked/unmasked learned tokens, excluding masked tokens from the loss) is clearly described.

A custom contrastive audio-visual synchronization model built on a large pretrained vision backbone (VideoPrism) is introduced, with a thoughtful analysis of why small batch sizes matter for synchronization (hard-negative argument), moving beyond reuse of Synchformer features.

Comprehensive evaluation: objective metrics (FAD, KL variants, IS, IB, DeSync) plus a human listening study; ablations of shortcut vs. flow matching at two model sizes (Table 2), few-step comparisons against the distilled Frieren reflow checkpoint (Table 3), long-form comparisons against LoVA (Table 5) and duration sweeps against MMAudio (Figure 4), and a parameter-scaling study up to 1.01B (Table 6). The result that the shortcut objective incurs no fidelity loss at full step counts is an important, well-supported finding.

Detailed appendix supporting reproducibility: VAE fine-tuning (43 Hz frame rate), full training hyperparameters, the SWSD metric with an explicit algorithm, and the human-study interface/protocol; the limitations section honestly discusses the scene-cut weakness of progressive outpainting.
weaknesses: Comparisons are conducted on the authors' own mixed-length test set rather than standard benchmarks used in prior work, with baselines re-evaluated under author-recommended settings; published numbers for baselines may not transfer, and readers cannot easily verify fairness of the comparison protocol. Some baselines (AudioX, LoVA, Frieren) have no human-evaluation entries, leaving the subjective comparison limited to MMAudio and FoleyCrafter.

The human study is small (18 participants x 10 videos = 180 scores, 60 per model), no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals on MOS differences are reported, and notably SALSA-V scores lower than MMAudio on the Audio Quality axis (2.96 vs 3.16), which softens the claim of overall superiority; the abstract emphasizes alignment/synchronization wins but the quality result deserves more discussion.

Reproducibility is undermined by an empty 'Project page:' link and no stated plan to release code, models, or the custom test set; a proprietary 'high-fidelity studio Foley set' used for training is not described or available, making exact reproduction infeasible.

There is a potential self-reinforcing data pipeline: the contrastive synchronization model trained on VGGSound is used to filter the ~900h training corpus, which may bias training data toward that model's notion of alignment; the effect of this filtering is not ablated.

Long-form evaluation protocol compares a chunked extension method (0.5s reference + 9.5s generation) against MMAudio processing the full sequence; while the authors discuss this asymmetry, the comparison of context access is not fully controlled, and the fixed 10s context means the model's own long-horizon consistency relies on the same outpainting mechanism whose scene-cut weakness is acknowledged.

Several choices are asserted from observation without ablation or evidence (e.g., 25% self-consistency ratio, the number of blocks n with audio self-attention, 8 FPS vs other frame rates for semantic features, CFG value 4.0), limiting insight into which design decisions drive the gains.

strengths: The application of the shortcut formulation (Frans et al., 2025) to video-to-audio generation is genuinely new and is well-motivated: Table 2 cleanly demonstrates that the shortcut objective incurs no fidelity loss at full sampling budgets (32 steps) versus a matched flow-matching variant, which is a meaningful advantage over distillation/reflow approaches that degrade multi-step quality.

Evaluation coverage is unusually broad for this area: objective distribution metrics, semantic and temporal alignment, a blind randomized human listening study (Section A.4 describes a careful protocol), generation-latency benchmarks (Table 4), an ablation across model sizes (Tables 2 and 6), few-step comparison against a dedicated distilled baseline (Table 3), and long-form evaluation against LoVA (Table 5).

The custom contrastive synchronization model built on a large pretrained vision backbone (VideoPrism) with AST is a sensible contribution, and the analysis of why small batch sizes matter for synchronization contrastive training (Section 3.1) is an interesting, non-obvious observation.

The masked flow-matching objective elegantly unifies audio conditioning/outpainting with long-form generation via iterative extension, and the appendix provides reproducible detail (Algorithm 1, CFG formulation, length unification with stop-gradient gating).
The limitations section is honest about the main weakness of the progressive outpainting approach (carrying over sound characteristics across scene cuts).
weaknesses: The headline claims of 'significantly outperforms' are not well supported by the margins in Table 1: DeSync improves from 0.521 (MMAudio) to 0.497 on a metric the paper itself states has 0.2-second resolution, and FAD improves 1.12 to 1.07. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any objective metric, and the human study (18 participants, 10 videos, 180 total scores) is small; differences of 3.43 vs 3.29 overall are likely within noise.

The evaluation test set is self-constructed (mixed-length in-the-wild, VGGSound, UnAV-100 up to 30s) rather than a standard benchmark, so Table 1 numbers are not comparable to any published results and cannot be externally verified; notably, AudioX and LoVA — which beat or match SALSA-V on several objective metrics — are excluded from the human evaluation, leaving only MMAudio and FoleyCrafter as subjective comparators.

There is a potential circularity concern: the training corpus (~900h) was filtered using the authors' own audio-visual synchronization model, and the primary selling-point metric (DeSync, computed with a synchronization model of the same family) may therefore be indirectly optimized by the data curation. The paper does not ablate this filtering choice.

The long-form comparison methodology in Figure 4 is somewhat apples-to-oranges: SALSA-V iteratively extends with a 0.5s reference while MMAudio processes full sequences, and the authors themselves acknowledge MMAudio would likely perform better up to 20s with full-sequence access. The 30s comparison (Table 5) against only LoVA is thin support for the 'unconstrained length' claim, and quality at 60s (Figure 4, right) visibly degrades.

Reproducibility is a material concern: the 'Project page' placeholder in Section 1 is empty, no code or model release is mentioned, a 'high-fidelity studio Foley set' used for both VAE fine-tuning and text supervision is not characterized or sourced, and the YouTube/Panda70M filtering pipeline is described only at a high level. Independent replication would be difficult.

The audio-conditioning claims (matching spectral characteristics of reference audio) rest largely on qualitative spectrogram figures plus a newly proposed SWSD metric evaluated only on 'a representative subset' of audios; there is no baseline comparison (e.g., against a text-only or unconditioned variant at matched setup) establishing that the mechanism outperforms simpler conditioning alternatives.

Component-wise, the contribution is largely an assembly of known techniques (MMDiT-X blocks, VampNet-style mask tokens, SigLIP loss, shortcut models); the novelty is in the combination and domain transfer, which is legitimate but modest, and the paper could better isolate which components drive the synchronization gains (no ablation of the custom sync features vs. off-the-shelf Synchformer conditioning in the generative model).

strengths: The paper addresses multiple well-motivated, practical limitations of current video-to-audio models simultaneously: long-form generation, audio conditioning/outpainting, and few-step sampling, and integrates them coherently into a single model rather than as separate post-hoc fixes.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: objective distribution-matching metrics (FAD, KL), semantic and temporal alignment metrics, generation-time comparisons, few-step comparisons against a dedicated distilled baseline (Frieren reflow), long-form comparisons against LoVA, a model-size/scaling ablation (Table 6), and a blind human listening study.

The shortcut objective is shown (Table 2) to incur essentially no fidelity penalty relative to a vanilla flow-matching variant at full sampling steps, which is a meaningful and clearly demonstrated advantage over distillation/reflow pipelines; the few-step comparison (Table 3, Figure 4) supports the central few-step claim.

The masked flow-matching design (learned mask/unmask tokens, loss restricted to noised tokens) is cleanly described, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail (VAE fine-tuning, sequence-length unification, contrastive model training, SWSD metric with full algorithm), supporting reproducibility of the method.

The discussion of batch-size effects in contrastive synchronization training (Section 3.1) is an interesting and honest empirical observation, and the limitations section candidly identifies the scene-cut weakness of progressive outpainting.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely an integration of existing techniques (shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025), masked outpainting in the style of VampNet/Chen et al., MMDiT-X, SigLIP-style contrastive sync features) applied to V2A. The paper claims 'first adoption' of shortcut models in generative audio, which is a relatively thin conceptual novelty for a main-track paper, and the custom contrastive sync model is architecturally close to prior Segment-AVCLIP/Synchformer work with a larger backbone.

Comparability of the headline results (Table 1) is weakened by evaluation on a custom mixed-length test set of the authors' own construction; prior work's numbers on standard fixed-duration benchmarks are not reported, so it is hard to verify the SOTA claims independently. The training set is also filtered using the authors' own synchronization model, which could systematically favor models aligned with the evaluation setup (DeSync is computed with Synchformer).

The human study is small: 18 participants, 10 videos, 180 total scores, and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the MOS comparisons; the differences between SALSA-V (3.43) and MMAudio (3.29) in overall quality are within plausible noise. Audio quality in the human study (2.96) is actually below MMAudio (3.16), which is under-discussed relative to the synchronization claims.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the 'Project page:' entry in the contribution list is empty, no code or model release is stated, and key details (exact model/VAE sizes in latent channels, test set composition and size, how baseline models were evaluated on variable-length inputs) are only partially specified. The 'high-fidelity studio Foley dataset' is described vaguely and its provenance/licensing is unclear.

The 'near-real-time' framing is somewhat overstated: at 4 steps SALSA-V takes 0.71 s for a 10-second sample, which is slower than Frieren's 0.12 s, and generation at 8+ steps is still well short of real-time throughput for interactive workflows; timing comparisons favor the much smaller Frieren model.

Several quantitative claims rest on qualitative evidence: the long-form audio-conditioning fidelity analysis (Section A.3) is evaluated on a 'representative subset' of unspecified size with a newly proposed metric (SWSD) validated only by its own consistency, and no listening study covers the audio-conditioning or long-form settings.
